title: ‘Scrubs’ Stars On How Scott Foley & Rachel Bilson’s Arrival Changes J.D. & Elliot’s Relationship & Impacts Turk’s Marriage
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Magic Of Returning To ‘Big Bang’ Stage, Going Multi-Cam In Meta Season 1 Finale & Season 2 Plans ‘The Beast In Me’ Renewed For Season 2 With Claire Danes Reprising Role; Howard Gordon Back With Netflix Overall Deal David Oyelowo & Viola Prettejohn To Star In ‘The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo’ TV Series For Sky View All September 25, 2026 7:30am Rachel Bilson and Scott Foley in 'Scrubs' Disney/Darko Sikman Exes J.D. ( Zach Braff ) and Elliot ( Sarah Chalke ) are both getting significant others in Season 2 of Scrubs ‘ revival on ABC, and for Elliot, it’s a blast from the past and someone J.D. was once jealous of. As Deadline revealed exclusively last month , Scott Foley is returning to the medical comedy, reprising his role as marine biologist Sean as he and Elliot rekindle their previous on-again off-again romance. And Rachel Bilson , whose hospital visitor Charlie hit it off with J.D. in the Season 1 finale , is also back for an arc as the duo hard launch their relationship that may be coming fast and furious for J.D. Related Stories News 'Scrubs' Stars On Joel Kim Booster & X Mayo's Departures, Ava Bunn's Promotion, J.D.'s New Foe & Giving Interns Their Own Episodes In Season 2 Casting Tamera Mowry-Housley To Guest Star On 'Scrubs' Season 2 “J.D. is going, as you said, a little fast and furious with her, and Turk’s giving him advice that he’s going way too fast and needs to calm down,” Braff said. Added Faison, “He’s a little rusty with his courtship, and he’s going all in a little too too much, but that makes Turk realize that he hasn’t been going in with the wife at all, as far as the romantic side goes. Like he’s just playing husband; I’ll come home, we’re gonna do the maybe watch a movie thing, and then let’s go to bed, and then I’ll go to work, and you go to work in the morning, and stuff like that. He’s not doing any type of romantic anything.” The first three episodes of Season 2 set up a “running storyline of the difference in all of our lives,” Braff said. “J.D. is a bachelor again, and he’s out there in a new exciting thing, Turk’s been in a long-term relationship for many years, and Elliot’s also dipping her toe in the dating waters,” he said. “The contrast between our romantic lives is something that’s really been funny. Scott Foley’s back to be a love interest for Sarah for some episodes, and Rachel’s been mine, and the dynamic with us all together is just hilarious, we’re having so much fun.” Besides revisiting a classic Scrubs love triangle (J.D., Elliot, Sean) that produced the signature “Nobody cares, Sean” line the jealous J.D. used to say, Foley’s return serves another story purpose. “The writers were like, ‘How do we bring back Elliot’s neuroses?’,” Chalke said. “And so they thought that Scott would be a good way to do that because now that Elliot’s more comfortable in her job and feels super confident as a doctor, this is kind of what shakes her and brings back a lot of her neurotic days.” This marks a character adjustment — and return to form — for Elliot. “One thing we overcorrected for a little bit in Season 1 was Elliot being this mature person, and not that she’s not mature, but I think I and Sarah and others and fans missed a little bit of batsh*t crazy Elliot. Said Chalke, “We brought some of the batsh*t back.” Added Braff, “So we’ve taken the batsh*t dial in Elliot and put it back to normal. And by normal, I mean her old batsh*t stuff. “Which has been super fun to do, I missed it,” Chalke said. Is Elliot getting back with Sean because she may be jealous of what J.D. has with Charlie, and what happened with her Season 1 romantic interest pilot Wes who doesn’t seem to be in the picture anymore? “We reference the fact that she’s still with the pilot at the beginning, but she doesn’t really realize, like Carla’s, like ‘Elliot, he’s so boring.’ She’s like, ‘He’s not boring, he’s just sending me pictures,’ and it was amazing the different alts of the jokes that the writers came up with for the photos that Wes was sending her. And then she realizes, she looks at what Charlie and J.D. have, and she’s like, ‘Huh, maybe I do want that’.” Braff applauded Elliot’s classy reaction to his new romance. “She’s being very mature about it, I have to say, because J.D.’s not being very tactful about his loving on Charlie. Added Chalke, “Yeah, it’s in her face, in the workplace and outside.” “Yeah, it’s not very respectful,” Braff continued. “But J.D.’s about to get a big wake-up call when TV’s Scott Foley shows up with his green eyes.” Added Faison, “He’s so handsome. He’s got like this salt and pepper thing going right now. title: ‘American Horror Story’ Is Back With 13: Here’s How All the Seasons Connect (So Far)
full_text: Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 25, 2026 7:27am Jessica Lange as Constance Langdon in 'American Horror Story: 13.' Eric Liebowitz/FX Logo text [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the first three episodes of American Horror Story season 13 , “13,” 1:13 AM” and “Rauhnacht.”] As Madison Montgomery ( Emma Roberts ) says, “Surprise, bitch!” American Horror Story is officially back for its 13th season — and so are many of the franchise’s most memorable characters, with a plethora of superstitions to come. Thursday night debuted the first three episodes of the highly anticipated season 13, introducing new character Ben (Joey Pollari) as the audience’s entry point to this twisted, crossover story. Ben fittingly has triskaidekaphobia, a fear of the number 13, though he can’t seem to escape it. Related Stories TV When and Where to Watch 'American Horror Story' Season 13 Online TV Ryan Murphy Says He Finished 'Glee' Reboot Script Despite his debilitating triskaidekaphobia, his greater fear is that his relationship with his Taylor Swift-superfan girlfriend, Kira (Madelaine Petsch), will crumble if he doesn’t attend her birthday trip on the 13th with 13 of her best friends. He ends up taking the flight, but the plane crashes, killing Kira and 12 of her friends. Ben survives, as does another passenger who was sitting in 13B. Ben was sitting in 13F. The crash is the first indication that the number 13 is more than just a superstition in the new season. As the first three episodes unfold, the number keeps appearing in increasingly sinister ways — ultimately helping connect the season’s seemingly disparate characters and storylines. Before getting to what appears to be the main setting of the season — an apartment building called the Apollyon in New York City — the episode flashes to Miss Robichaux’s Academy for Exceptional Young Ladies, where Supreme Cordelia ( Sarah Paulson ) and Madison of season three’s Coven are helping newbie Ophelia (Avantika) work on her telepathy. This is where Madison makes her iconic grand entrance: “Surprise, bitch! This witch approves.” A storm is happening, however, hinting that we’re in the same timeline as the plane crash. Cordelia senses something sinister approaching. “So much vengeful death,” she says. “Something wicked this way comes.” With so many stars returning for the 13th installment and reprising their roles, Ryan Murphy had clarified to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of its release that this season is not a sequel; instead, “It’s a different story with characters that you love returning.” “They’re fighting a very big villain,” he said of the returning stars. “There has to be something big enough that even the ones who were villains before are now heroes — they’re united against a force that we’ve touched on in other seasons, but not in the way we are doing this season. There’s a big villain.” That villain remains a mystery after the first three episodes, but the story increasingly points toward the mysterious Mr. Nas. Fedor Steer as Mr. Nas. Eric Liebowitz/FX A month following the plane crash, Ben arrives at the Apollyon and meets the one-and-only Constance Langdon ( Jessica Lange ), who lives on the 13th floor and is apparently no longer tethered to the infamous Murder House from season one. She introduces Ben to Nas, played by Fedor Steer, who portrays the character in his older years. Paul Anthony Kelly plays Young Nas. Constance says Nas is 87, and Ben becomes his caregiver. Pollari told THR that Lange took him under her wing, as he’s a newcomer this season. “We are close off screen as well, and the scenes that we have together really developed a bond,” he said at the show’s New York premiere . “I learned a lot from her.” During the time of the plane crash, Nas is shown coughing up a strange black substance at the same time . Could Nas be the ultimate villain Murphy is referring to? The connection only becomes more suspicious in the second episode. After Ben discovers a series of strange references to the number 13 throughout Nas’ penthouse, including 13 figures in a depiction of The Last Supper , the episode cuts to Los Angeles, where Twisty the Clown (John Carroll Lynch), the serial killer clown from season four’s Freak Show , arrives at a clown school and proceeds to massacre 13 people at the school, including the teacher played by Tig Notaro. Back at the Apollyon, Nas vomits the same black, viscous substance again. The episode therefore appears to establish a connection between Nas and the deaths, though exactly what that connection is remains unclear. Ben also continues to question why Constance is caring for Nas. She reveals that all of her children are “alive and thriving,” which leads to one of the season’s biggest surprises: the return of her daughter Adelaide (Jamie Brewer), who is back “in this mortal coil.” The reunion becomes even stranger when Constance prepares for a dark holiday celebration, with Kai Anderson ( Evan Peters ) from Cult helping decorate a black Christmas tree topped with a pentagram. Constance’s son, Tate Langdon (also Peters), is there as well, with Peters playing both characters in the same scene. Joey Pollari as Ben, Jessica Lange as Constance Langdon. Eric Liebowitz/FX The gathering then grows into a supernatural AHS reunion in the third episode. Winter Anderson (Billie Lourd) from Cult arrives with a masked friend who is revealed to be Elizabeth Short, aka the Black Dahlia (Mena Suvari), from Murder House . Lourd — who first joined the Murphy-verse in 2015 for Scream Queens, which she hopes is revived — appeared in season seven’s Cult alongside Peters’ Kai. Of reuniting with the star, she told THR, “Evan is my brother from another mother. I love that man so much. We have so much fun together.” For the dark holiday scene, Lourd said she watched Peters put on his Rubber Man suit. “I did feel bad for him, having to be in that latex suit though. I watched him get lubed up and into it one day,” she said. During the reunion, Constance tells Elizabeth that she will become one of “13 lucky leading ladies,” adding yet another ominous reference to the number. Of season 13 bringing everyone together, Suvari told THR, “It’s really for all of the fans that have been so loving about this show along the way.” But the gathering has a larger purpose. The holiday is Rauhnacht, a period when the veil between Hell and Earth is at its thinnest. After Constance’s party, Winter, Kai, Tate and Adelaide take Elizabeth to a speakeasy called Club Hell. When they reach the basement of the Apollyon, Wilhemina Venable (Sarah Paulson) from season eight’s Apocalypse meets them, marking Paulson’s second character entrance, and welcomes them to what she calls a portal to Hell. The episode ends before revealing exactly what Constance and the others have planned for Elizabeth, though the references to sacrifices and the group’s plans for the 13 “leading ladies” suggest that she is being prepared for some kind of ritual. That leaves the first three episodes with a much larger mystery than simply why so many familiar faces have returned. The season appears to be building toward a supernatural conflict that connects the worlds — and timelines — of several previous American Horror Story installments. Evan Peters as Kai Anderson. Eric Liebowitz/FX As audiences wait for more episodes to drop weekly, Leslie Grossman, another regular in Murphy shows who is set to reprise Coco St. Pierre Vanderbilt from Apocalypse, explained how the seasons connect. “It is one big universe, but there’s many different timelines, and we have taken great care to make sure that all of the timelines intersect in a way that makes sense and is very satisfying for the fanbase,” she told THR. “So remember, all one universe, different timelines and they’re going to intersect in ways that are surprising.” She added, “I have to tell you, I read scripts and I was like, ‘No way! I had no idea that was going to happen.’ There are many Easter eggs and a lot of good payoff if you’ve been a fan of the show, but you can also have not watched it before, and I think you’re going to still enjoy this season.” After three episodes, big questions remain: Who exactly is Nas? Why does he seem connected to the deaths surrounding the number 13? Why has Constance brought these particular characters back together? And what exactly is waiting beneath the Apollyon? Oh, and is Ben really alive? *** New episodes of AHS: 13 premiere Thursdays on FX . Read all of THR’s coverage here . THR

title: Shemar Moore Is Back in Action in Starz’s Solid Cop Drama ‘S.W.A.T. Exiles’: TV Review
full_text: Sep 25, 2026 7:15am PT Shemar Moore Is Back in Action in Starz’s Solid Cop Drama ‘S.W.A.T. Exiles’: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review 4 days ago ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Proves the Show Just Wouldn’t Work Without Tom Hardy 7 days ago Netflix’s ‘Monster’ Finally Delivers an Outrageously Engaging Season With ‘The Lizzie Borden Story’: TV Review 1 week ago See All Kit Karzen/Sony Pictures Televis Just one year after wrapping an eight-season run on CBS’ “S.W.A.T.,” Shemar Moore ’s stoic but righteous Sergeant II Daniel “Hondo” Harrelson Jr. returns on a new network in the spinoff series “ S.W.A.T. Exiles .” Created by Jason Nig, the Starz show is set two years after the original series ended, and Hondo is in a very different place. Divorced and alone, he has also been ousted from the LAPD following a botched raid that ended with the death of one of his young squad members. These days, Hondo is a reluctant bodyguard for some of Los Angeles’ most insufferable billionaire tech bros, but his luck changes when LAPD Commander Robert Hicks (Patrick St. Esprit, reprising his role) offers him the opportunity to command a new unit. Deeply resentful following his forced retirement, Hondo begrudgingly takes the new position, but soon realizes he’s being set up to fail. A solid sequel to a well-liked procedural, “S.W.A.T Exiles” uses many of the same tricks that made the original show so popular. Yet, with a brand-new team and a handful of compelling storylines, the show proves it can stand on its own. The 10-episode first season (four episodes were available for review) opens on an ordinary day in LA., where audiences get a glimpse of Hondo’s empty house. Aside from dirty dishes and a calendar covered in his young daughter’s doodles, there are few signs of life. He moves on autopilot, bitter about the past and working out his anguish with endless push-ups. Each day blends into the next, so when Hicks offers him the chance to suit up again, he decides he can’t pass it up. Yet almost as soon as he enters his new headquarters, Hondo recognizes this new role isn’t what it seems. It’s clear the LAPD has an image problem, and they’ve trotted him out yet again to fix it. Additionally, the short-tempered leader has been given an unpredictable Gen Z team who are difficult to corral. Among the new 44 Squad, which Hondo aptly calls the Exiles, is Sammy Bishop (Lucy Barrett), a gun expert and social media star who, much to Hondo’s horror, has no qualms about live-streaming from headquarters. Malik Henderson (Adain Bradley), a Marine veteran and devoted husband and father, appears most suited for the job, especially when Hondo makes him Scout, or the point person for missions. (Malik has some skeletons in his closet, though.) Ethan Cole (Freddy Miyares) is a neurodivergent tech savant who picks up on way more than people give him credit for. Cassidy Han (Zyra Gorecki) is intense, disciplined and determined not to let her prosthetic leg define her, but her reserved nature makes her a mystery to her colleagues. The recruits are rounded out by Jude Callan (Ronen Rubinstein), a charming, cocky bad boy with unexpected depth. At the start, Hondo flexes his rusty leadership skills and tries to get his ragtag crew to work as a cohesive unit. Still, despite the typical procedural formula with cases tied to gun smugglers, cartel assassins and kidnappings, the show remains topical enough to keep viewers engaged. When Hondo realizes his team is being undermined and someone on the inside is feeding information to the mayor’s office to take him down, the stakes for “S.W.A.T. Exiles” become more intriguing. While this conspiracy runs across the entire first season, the reveal of who’s behind it isn’t as straightforward as one might expect. “S.W.A.T Exiles” isn’t as fixed or formulaic as other action-dramas. Episode 4, “Get Clear,” is a gem in the season. Instead of taking audiences through yet another mission, Hondo and the team are called before the Force Review Board to testify about a prior bungled assignment. Cutting back and forth between the present and the past, each member of the unit reflects on a hostage situation turned ICE raid that went completely off track, leaving an unarmed civilian shot dead by Hondo’s hand. As the officers recall the incident, Hondo focuses on finding out who the mole is and how to proceed with this information. When it’s all said and done, “S.W.A.T. Exiles” doesn’t reinvent the wheel for its genre, or even from the previous series. But Moore is commanding and earnest as he steps back into Hondo’s shoes, this time, to shepherd a new generation of officers who are also trying to navigate their pasts and personal lives. And it looks like Starz believes in the franchise, since “S.W.A.T. Exiles” has already been greenlit for Season 2. The film, which opened to warm Zurich audiences last night, will have a limited theatrical release in the U.S. from Oct. 9 ahead of its global streaming debut on Apple TV on Oct. 16. “The only problem is that the audience comes mainly from three, four huge movies,” he said of this year’s record-breaking $4.76 billion U.S. summer box office, driven largely by Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and Destin Daniel Cretton’s “ Spider-Man : Brand New Day.” “A couple of smaller movies kind of catch on and do well, but it’s got to be spread out a little bit.” Related Stories Three Films, and a Second Oscar? Popular on Variety Speaking about his turn in the comic book world, Dafoe said he became a part of it at the “start of business-as-normal making movies from comic books.” “When I was proposed this role, some of my friends were like: ‘Are you kidding? Are you going to play this green guy? That’s not cool! That sounds like a terrible movie!’” “I was not a big comic book fan; I didn’t know about this world, but Sam Raimi did,” he added. “I saw his attachment to it and saw how he saw it. I liked him so much that he really is what got me into it. Once I was in it, I had really fun things to do.” The actor said he “had done some movies that had found success” but that, to this day, the most consistent point of recognition from audiences is “probably the Green Goblin.” “For better or for worse,” he said. “Luckily, I do other things so I am not haunted by this mono-identity, but it’s pretty strong.” Dafoe enjoyed his experience in the Marvel Cinematic Universe both in the 2002 film and during his return as Green Goblin on “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” “They’re part of cinema. They are right up there with Bela Tarr,” he quipped. Apple Original Films “Tenzing” chronicles the story of the first-ever ascent of Mount Everest by Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary, played by Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston, respectively. Dafoe plays Colonel John Hunt, the leader of the 1953 British expedition team. Commenting on the experience of shooting on real mountains at high altitude, Dafoe said the entire film team had to be “very careful.” “We had great safety people,” he noted. “They’re checking for avalanches, for all sorts of things. There are 10 guys purely helping us slip in and making sure we’re safe, helping us if we struggle […] That’s the tension. Courtesy of Maria Farinha Filmes Oscar-nominated Italian producer Donatella Palermo (“Fire at Sea,” “Caesar Must Die”) has boarded Eryk Rocha’s highly anticipated doc “ Elza ” as a production associate. The film will have its world premiere at the Rio Film Festival and its international premiere at the Rome Film Festival . “Elza” is the follow-up to Rocha’s “The Falling Sky,” which premiered to great acclaim at Directors’ Fortnight. The film is a comprehensive documentary about one of Brazil ’s most renowned singers and public figures, Elza Soares. Drawing on rare archival materials and intimate conversations between Soares and the director during the final years of her life, “Elza” traces the icon’s seven-decade career while revealing the many facets of the woman behind the legend. The project comes with the backing of high-calibre partners, including Aruac Filmes (“Cinema Novo”), Maria Farinha Filmes (“The Beginning of Life”), Globo Filmes (“I’m Still Here”), RAI Cinema and Gullane +. How Penélope Cruz Could Dominate Awards Season With 'La Bola Negra,' 'The Invite' and 'Bunker' Rocha, who followed Elza over eight years of filming, said: “Elza Soares is a beacon whose art and legacy continue to guide us. To tell her story is also to tell the story of our country. By allowing Elza to tell her story in her own voice, the film brings us once again into the presence of this immense woman and artist.” Popular on Variety “The film is also a way to honor her dedication to music and her commitment to everything she was, and everything she continues to represent,” he added. “I am deeply moved to share this film with audiences and to have Elza’s voice sing once again, for Brazil and the entire world.” Soares’s work intersected with some of the defining figures in international music, from Argentine tango composer and arranger Astor Piazzolla to jazz legends Louis Armstrong and Ella Fitzgerald. Soares met Armstrong in Chile in 1962, during a World Cup that would change the course of her life. Named BBC’s “Voice of the Millennium,” Elza transcended genres and national borders to become a global symbol of artistic freedom, resilience, and the enduring power of Black women’s voices. Her death in 2022 moved the entire country, with artists and fans paying lengthy homages to the trailblazer. “Elza” is produced by Aruac Filmes and Maria Farinha Filmes, in co-production with Globo Filmes and GloboNews. The film is distributed by Gullane+ and Maria Farinha Filmes. The film was produced in collaboration with Faber Produzioni and RAI Cinema. “Elza” is supported by the City of São Paulo, through Spcine, and by Itaú Cultural, and was produced with funding from the Brazilian Federal Government, through the Aldir Blanc National Policy for the Promotion of Culture (PNAB), in coordination with the National Culture System, with investment from the Audiovisual Sector Fund, and with institutional support from the Ministry of Culture and Ancine. title: Dolly Parton, Lily Tomlin & Jane Fonda Film ‘9 To 5’ Gets One-Week Screen Return For Parton Charity

title: Warner Music Names Val Blavatnik to Executive Team, Unveils Suite of Leadership Promotions
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All September 25, 2026 7:00am Atlantic Music Group CEO Elliot Grainge, and WMG managing director Val Blavatnik. Monica Schipper/Getty Images Warner Music Group announced a suite of leadership changes Friday morning that most notably has Val Blavatnik, son of the company’s majority shareholder Len Blavatnik, officially joining WMG’s executive team as managing director of North America, U.K. and corporate development. Industry insiders had been anticipating the younger Blavatnik’s entry into the company for years , and speculation of his impending appointment had been growing louder over the past several months. As managing director, WMG said Blavatnik, who is also on WMG’s board of directors, would “unify and drive business and operational strategy across these markets while guiding the company’s investment strategy to support growth.” Outside of Blavatnik’s new role, Atlantic Music Group CEO Elliot Grainge has also been named chairman of WMG’s distribution service ADA, and he is appointing Atlantic COO Zach Friedman as ADA’s vice chairman. With Warner Records COO Tom Corson recently being promoted to WMG COO, Aaron Bay-Schuck has been named sole chairman and CEO of Warner Records Group. Warner Music Latin America President Alejandro Duque, who had previously been named president of ADA last year, has been elevated to President of Warner Music International, where he’ll now also oversee the APAC and EMEA regions. Warner Music Iberia exec Guillermo Gonzalez has been upped to president of Warner Music EMEA, with Andrés Rothschild succeeding him as president of Warner Music Iberia. “To build upon our successful year in which we delivered on all three strategic priorities to grow market share, increase the value of music and increase our efficiency, these frontline executive changes enhance our best-in-class leadership team with diverse skill sets to execute on the next chapter of WMG’s growth,” WMG CEO Robert Kyncl said in a statement. “Elliot, Aaron, Alejandro and Guillermo are exceptional, dynamic and proven leaders who have transformed their domains, and elevating them allows us to further scale their success. I’m also excited to welcome Val to the executive team, where his operational and strategic focus will help us build our momentum across key markets.” As part of the shakeup, WMG executive Simon Robson, who’s been at the company for nearly 30 years, will step down in December to “pursue new opportunities.” “We owe a tremendous debt of gratitude to Simon Robson for his dedicated service, operational excellence and trusted leadership while expanding WMG’s global footprint over his remarkable tenure, and wish him the very best in his next endeavors,” Kyncl said. The wide swath of executive moves is just the latest in a particularly notable c-suite shakeup at WMG over the past several years. Former WMG CFO Armin Zerza confirmed he’d be departing from the company in July, with his eventual successor set to become the company’s fourth CFO since 2023. Meanwhile, earlier this week, WMG had announced that Warner Chappell COO and co-chair Carianne Marshall was departing as well , with Guy Moot set to become the publisher’s sole chairman. THR

title: New York Film Festival Boss on Scoring ‘Artificial’ and ‘Behemoth’ World Premieres and Why Movies Are ‘Unavoidably Political’
full_text: Sep 25, 2026 7:00am PT New York Film Festival Boss on Scoring ‘Artificial’ and ‘Behemoth’ World Premieres and Why Movies Are ‘Unavoidably Political’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Paige DeSorbo on Leaving ‘Summer House’ Behind and Speaking Out About a Past Abusive Relationship: ‘Domestic Violence’ Can ‘Truly Happen to Anyone’ 2 days ago ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Could Top Box Office, Brad Pitt’s ‘Heart of the Beast’ and Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ Vie for No. 3 2 days ago ‘Evita’ on Broadway: West End Stars Diego Rodriguez, James Olivas to Reprise Roles Alongside Rachel Zegler (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All From the surprise election of mayor Zohran Mamdani to the Knicks winning the NBA championship, it’s been a time for underdog stories in the Big Apple. The New York Film Festival is continuing the trend, pulling off a coup by securing several major world premieres in a year that’s been frustratingly light on festival fanfare. NYFF starts on Sept. 25, and over the next two weeks, audiences will be the first to watch “ Artificial ,” Luca Guadagnino’s buzzy movie about OpenAI founder Sam Altman; “A Statement,” director Tom McCarthy’s starry drama about climate change; “Behemoth,” Tony Gilroy’s ode to film scores led by Pedro Pascal; “14th,” Ava DuVernay’s timely documentary about the 14th Amendment; and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” a kaiju sequel to Oscar-winner “Godzilla Minus One.” It’s an exciting change of pace for the small-but-mighty NYFF, whose lineup is often comprised of the buzziest movies from Cannes, Venice or Toronto. Related Stories Penélope Cruz Sobs and Kisses Javier Bardem as ‘Bunker’ Dazzles Venice With Record 15.5-Minute Ovation ‘Day Drinker’ Trailer: Johnny Depp's Hollywood Comeback Continues in a Twisty Thriller With Penélope Cruz and Madelyn Cline “Premiere status is never the be-all and end-all for us,” says NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim. “But I think we’ve proved in the last few years that we create a pretty interesting context for the launch of a film.” Popular on Variety Many of these films tackle hot-button issues that speak to these politically fraught times. But that’s not to say that everything on this year’s lineup is fire and brimstone. There are fun and joyous movies, too, Lim points out, citing Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy “Club Kid” and Jesse Eisenberg’s musical drama “The Debut.” Ahead of this year’s festival, Lim spoke to Variety about lining up so many heavy hitters and whether festivalgoers should be prepared for any surprises. NYFF is hosting several buzzy world premieres. Was that a priority? There is more than usual this year. It’s just a confluence of factors. Timing is always part of it. We are a month after the major fall festivals: Telluride, Venice, and Toronto. We’re not a competitive festival. It doesn’t make sense for us to have world premieres be the majority of our program. But I’m very excited about each of the world premieres. How did you get “Artificial” on the lineup? There was chatter that it might skip the festival circuit entirely. That was genuinely an up-in-the-air situation. It was with a different studio until very recently , and it was an open conversation of whether this would do festivals. Luca is a filmmaker we have a relationship with, and I thought we would be a great launchpad for the film. This is a film that deals with a very pressing situation. AI is in the news practically daily. The film recaps this trajectory that we’ve been on with alarming clarity. And it does this in the form of an incredibly entertaining movie. It has a very dark humor, which is certainly one valid way of approaching the dystopian present. Tom McCarthy’s climate change drama “A Statement” wasn’t on many people’s radars. How did that come together? We knew the film might be ready. We saw it very late in the process. It fits exactly what I was saying about films that are tackling contemporary realities. We’ve just lived through some kind of climate apocalypse in most parts of the world this summer, and much in the same way that “Artificial” does with the AI crisis, this film is looking at a very specific moment in time with this climate conference from 1980. It explains why it’s so hard for action to be taken, despite very clear evidence. There’s been a lot of debate recently about the place of politics at film festivals. At Venice, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal called films “fundamentally, unavoidably political.” What is your take? I’d agree with that statement. I think all films are political. Even to say that one is apolitical is kind of a political position to take. To be human, to be alive in the world, is political. Cinema of all the art forms is unavoidably political. We’re reflecting the world; we’re responding to the world. The most urgent, meaningful films today are engaged with the realities of contemporary existence. Which film on the lineup surprised you the most? That’s a really tough one. Maybe “Behemoth,” Tony Gilroy’s film, another world premiere, because even though he’s been very active, he hasn’t made a feature film in a while. It was so clearly a passion project, and it has such a clear point of view. This is a film that makes clear that music isn’t just an accompaniment in the background of a film but a narrative device. We also try to make room for what you might call smaller films in the main slate, and those are often, for me, the most surprising. There are a couple of titles that have really stayed with me. “The Loneliest Man in Town” by Tikovian Rainer Frimmel, an Austrian film that’s a really lovely character study, and Nicholas Pareda’s film’s “Everything Else Is Noise,” a Mexican film by I think one of the most interesting filmmakers working today. It’s important for us to create the possibility for discovery and surprise for the audience, so we balance out the higher profile films with these other titles. One of the buzziest moments of last year’s festival was the surprise screening of “Marty Supreme.” Will there be surprises for festival attendees? “Marty” was a very exciting moment for us. I think that might account for the larger-than-usual number of world premieres in the lineup. I don’t think we will or need to do a surprise every year. It has to be the right film. A surprise that ends up being anticlimactic doesn’t serve anyone. We’re not wedded to the surprise thing. It’s not an annual tradition. But I think we will have evenings this year that will certainly rival the excitement of the “Marty Supreme” night. NYFF doesn’t have jury prizes. Will that ever change? As long as I have any say, there will not be competitions. So many filmmakers have told me that one of the reasons they truly enjoy their time at New York is the instant removal of stress of not having a competition. That changes everything when you’re a filmmaker and you have this pressure of: Will you get called back? Will you win? What does it mean to win or not win? It makes sense for premier festivals to have competitions, but I don’t think, in the context of how we’re currently configured, a competition would add anything. How do you survive long festival days, or when you have to screen multiple movies in one day? I wish I knew… that would make it easier. [Laughs] . I’ve actually gone back to watch films multiple times because when I’m in that state, you have to acknowledge that you’re losing your perspective. You know what it’s like to be at a festival and have a three or four film day, and it’s like you don’t trust your judgement. [Laughs] . For me, not doing anything screen related is the only way to reset. Caffeine also helps. You were crowned by GQ as the best dressed man at last year’s festival. How much thought do you put into your outfits? It’s a long festival! It’s just about being aware that you’re on stage with people who have stylists and budgets, and you don’t want to look like a slob. But it is a long festival … 15 days. It’s something I should probably start thinking about soon. (Additionally, Tamera Mowry-Housley will guest star as Dr. Steffie, a pediatric doctor.) Related Stories Casting Tamera Mowry-Housley To Guest Star On 'Scrubs' Season 2 News Imagen Awards: 'Acapulco' Leads As 'Brownsville Bred,' 'Will Trent' & 'Scrubs' Take Top Prizes - Full List Braff explained to Deadline the rationale behind Park’s departure and Grant’s arrival as a way to replicate the dynamic between Braff’s J.D. and Dr. Cox (John C. McGinley) on the original series, crediting Scrubs creator Bill Lawrence with the idea for the change-up. “Joel was incredible,” Braff said. “I think that we wanted to try and find a nemesis for J.D. who was underneath him. Bill Lawrence had this idea that that, well, there’s no one above J.D. except an administrator, and we’ve seen that before. It might be fun if the person driving him nuts is coming from underneath him, a chief resident, and so that was rethinking where the thorn in J.D.’s side is. “Obviously JD needs conflict, right, for the story to work, things are going very well for J.D., that’ll get boring quick. We need some conflict for drama and comedy, and I think the notion was: what if we introduce a fun thorn in his side, who is actually underneath him and drives him nuts, in the same way that J.D. drove Dr. Cox nuts.” Enter Higgins’ Grant. Mayo’s exit was particularly surprising as charge nurses Dubois (Michael James Scott) and Raymond (Mayo) were two of the revival’s breakout characters in Season 1. Turns out the departure was not story-driven but logistical. “We would have loved to have X on more,” Braff said. “She’s just working so much and so busy, and wasn’t really fully available. But we are bringing in more nurses and more characters. Michael James Scott really just popped, we all love him so much. He’s so friggin’ funny. Every single line he says on the show makes us all laugh, and so he really, really is shining. The writers keep writing to him, and I can’t imagine an episode without him. He’s so lovely to be around, and such a good actor.” The reason Mayo’s schedule came into play is that she and most of the Scrubs cast are recurring guest stars. As such, they are not under contracts and their services are subject to availability. Bunn’s Promotion In Season 1 of the revival, only Braff, Faison and Chalke were series regulars. They are being joined in Season 2 by Ava Bunn , who has been promoted from a recurring. She plays one of the new interns, Sam Tosh. “I think the Ava Bunn storyline — she plays Tosh on the show — is something that needs to be explored,” Faison said. “I don’t know if you’re on social media, but we’re on social media, and a lot of my diagnoses come from the doctors on social media or the things that they say, and that’s something to talk about. That is a new wave of getting information. Google used to be the way to do it, I’m going to Google all of my ailments and see what happens. Now it’s a new era, and a lot of people get their information from things like Instagram or Meta or ChatGPT. So, adding her to the show as the fourth in all of this is, she popped last year, and so here we go, and we’re excited for her too. This is something new.” Added Chalke, “Yeah, she’s great. She comes in with such great ideas, she’s improving all the time, and never delivers the same line twice. She has such confidence in her own skin for such a young age. It’s really cool.” Changing Interns’ Narrative — But Not Series’ Narrator Bunn’s character Sam Tosh got more attention than other new characters last season as she emerged as a wide-eyed intern standout in the vein of J.D. from the first eight seasons and Lucy (Kerry Bishé) from Season 9. Does Bunn’s promotion to a series regular signal a handover of narrator duties from J.D. to Tosh like it happened with him and Lucy in Season 9? “No. It’s interesting. The old show was about the interns, right? Well, now the show is about us,” Braff said, “So, unlike that Season 9, the show is not going to pivot to being about a new cast of interns.” With returning Scrubs fan favorites taking the spotlight, the show has not been able to sufficiently service the new cast, with most interns yet to make an impression as we know very little about them. The series is looking to correct that in Season 2. “One thing we did last year was we tried to service all the interns in every episode, and I think what we learned was we didn’t have the time in 21 minutes to really give them enough story,” Braff said. “So this year, we’re not putting each intern in every episode, but giving them their own episodes to shine, and I think that’s a better strategy for the audience, getting their claws into them and getting to know them better and embracing them more. With the exception of Ava, who’s been made a regular and she’ll be in every episode.” Mentors & Mentees For medical intern Tosh and surgical intern Dashana Trainor (Amanda Morrow), main storylines have been their relationships with mentors Elliot and Turk, respectively. “For Elliot, she picks up again in Season 2, where she’s mentoring Tosh, and, obviously, they’ve all become such great doctors and are really looking forward to this new chapter of being mentors,” Chalke said about Elliot, J.D. and Turk. “Elliot had a bit of a journey last season trying to figure out the balance of how do you mentor this kid who’s way too hard on her, and then pulled back, and is now giving her some more rope and recognizing what a good doctor she is and is becoming.” Said Faison, “With Turk, Dashana is already an example of excellence, she’s already at the top of her game, she’ll have Turk’s job in a few years. She’s that good of a surgeon, that good of a doctor already. And so I think Turk is taking her for granted. She’s making his life a lot easier, and he’s not even paying attention to it because he’s so stuck in his own mental health issues. So he’s got somebody there who should be inspiring him like no other, but he can’t see past his own reflection in the mirror to see that this girl is everything that he’s been asking for, and so, whereas these guys are thriving, being mentors for their doctors, he’s not even paying attention to how good she is.” Scrubs Season 2 launches on Sept. 30 with a two-episode premiere on ABC and streaming next day on Hulu. ‘Avengers: Endgame: Encore’ & ‘Primetime’ Eye $3M Previews ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’, Meta Finale & Season 2 Judge Grants Suit Settlement Delay; Company Proceeds With $7.5B Debt Raise David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi; WBD’s CNN, MS Now Denied Access To Event Read More About: Comments

title: Rio Fest’s RioMarket, Kicking Off Oct. 1, to Feature TikTok Program and Online Business Meetings
full_text: Sep 25, 2026 6:59am PT Rio Fest’s RioMarket, Kicking Off Oct. 1, to Feature TikTok Program and Online Business Meetings Amid a strong presence of Asian countries, RioMarket is launching an app to connect international film markets By Marcelo Cajueiro Plus Icon Marcelo Cajueiro Latest Grace Passô’s ‘Our Secret’ Nabs the Best Film Kikito at the 54th Gramado Film Festival 1 month ago ‘Seduction,’ Helmed by Zelito Viana and Marcos Palmeira, to Premiere at the Inffinito Fest in Miami (EXCLUSIVE) 1 month ago Gramado Targets Next-Gen Talent as Permanent Growth Engine (EXCLUSIVE) 1 month ago See All Walkiria Barbosa Credit Eny Miranda RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — RioMarket , the business section of the Rio International Film Festival, will be held over Oct. 1-11, featuring for the first time a partnership with TikTok and online one-on-one business meetings. The event, taking place in a warehouse in Rio’s port area renovated for the 2016 Summer Olympics, will gather execs and talents of the local and international film industry, with a strong presence of Asian countries, and will launch an app to connect festival film markets around the world. Related Stories Spain’s National Film Prize Honoree Carmen Machi: ‘Acting Has Been the Driving Force of My Happiness and Also a Balm for My Darkest Moments’ Penélope Cruz Sobs and Kisses Javier Bardem as ‘Bunker’ Dazzles Venice With Record 15.5-Minute Ovation The first online one-on-one business meetings were held at RioMarket 2025 and proved successful, Walkiria Barbosa , the Rio Film Festival ‘s executive director and head of international marketing, told Variety . Popular on Variety “We ran a pilot last year, and we are going to expand it this year. During the pandemic, we learned that it is possible to do business online,” she said. “We received applications from companies in several countries, including film and television production companies, streaming platforms, distributors, and television networks,” she said. One of the new features of RioMarket 2026 is a partnership with TikTok, Barbosa said. The social media giant will hold at the event a three-day workshop for 40 TikTok content creators invited by the company from several states in Brazil. The program’s aim is to improve the quality of the content they produce through technical sessions on directing, lighting, editing, screenwriting, format development, filming, and other areas of individual content production. “The goal is to raise the quality of entertainment content production on TikTok by connecting creators with experienced audiovisual professionals. We believe Festival do Rio, which brings together the leading players in Brazil’s entertainment industry, is the ideal setting to launch this new model,” Luciana Galastri, head of entertainment partnerships at TikTok in Latin America, told Variety . Luciana Galastri. Courtesy TikTok Barbosa stressed the strong presence at RioMarket 2026 of Asian countries, particularly China, India and South Korea, as well as Russia. Over the past years, Brazilian companies are increasingly doing more business with players from these countries, while maintaining the traditional interaction with partners in the North and Latin America and Europe, she said. From China, one of the highlights is the lecture of Spike Liu, president of China Year Technology. He will present experiences on the use of AI in content creation and production processes in the audiovisual sector. RioMarket will profit from the presence of international players in the soft launch of its app, which aims to connect film festivals’ markets around the world. Tentatively named Connecting Screens, the platform is inspired by Cinando, the online networking and business platform for film and audiovisual professionals run by Cannes’ Marché du Film. Connecting Screens will facilitate business meetings and provide info about projects, among many other features, Pedro Souza, president of the Financing Committee of the Audiovisual Industry and Commerce Federation (FICA), told Variety . “While Cinando resembles Wikipedia, our app will be a sort of Tinder, Linkedin and Wikipedia. The idea is to match sellers and buyers of the audiovisual industry,” Souza said. Photo Ilda Santiago . Credit Phil Lavra Apple Photos Clean Up Ilda Santiago, Rio Fest’s exec director of programing and international projects, stressed the importance of forming a new generation of moviegoers for the festival. RioMarket 2026 will count with the presence of participants of the Generation Program, Rio Fest’s initiative dedicated to the use of films in fostering education for children and teenagers in Rio. Santiago also underscored the significance of RioMarket: “The market feeds the festival program, and the program, in turn, feeds the market. Today, no major film festival can afford to operate without a strong industry market.” One of the most promising panels of RioMarket 2026 is the one that will put, face to face, two of the most critically acclaimed film directors in the world: Iran’s Asghar Farhadi , of “Parallel Tales” (2026), “A Separation (2011)” and “About Elly” (2009), and Brazilian Walter Salles , of “I’m Still Here” (2024), “Central Station” (1998) and “The Motorcycle Diaries” (2004). Another important panel is the one on LatAm Content Meeting, the Brazilian version of the Sunny Side of the Doc. Fernando Dias, the event’s founder, will provide information for non-fiction content makers interested in participating in the next edition of LatAm Content Meeting, in September 2027 in São Paulo. There will also be two panels presenting successful cases of international co-production of documentaries resulting from deals initiated in the first two editions of LatAm Content Meeting in 2025 and 2026. In addition, content analyst Gustavo Martínez will host a workshop centered on his approach to conflict structure in screenplays, which is based on Newton’s Third Law of Motion and aims to create points of tension and release so the audience remains engaged. “We are holding an event on the scale of the markets at the world’s leading international film festivals,” said Barbosa, who is also the president of FICA. She believes there is an opportunity for the growth of the Brazilian audiovisual industry. “Our goal is to triple the industry’s share of Brazil’s GDP over the next five years. It currently stands at 0.6%. We aim to achieve this by strengthening our companies, increasing the number of movie theaters, advancing technological development and expanding exports of Brazilian productions,” Barbosa said. title: Turkish Distributor Baska Sinema Boards AI-Generated Feature ‘A Woman Asleep’ for Theatrical Release (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 25, 2026 6:35am PT Turkish Distributor Baska Sinema Boards AI-Generated Feature ‘A Woman Asleep’ for Theatrical Release (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Turkish Distributor Baska Sinema Boards AI-Generated Feature ‘A Woman Asleep’ for Theatrical Release (EXCLUSIVE) 56 minutes ago ‘Percy Jackson’ Season 3 Stars Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries Set to Attend Italy’s Lucca Comics and Games 1 day ago Gaza Documentary ‘NAZA’ Set to Stream for Free on The Guardian Website After Global Release 1 day ago See All Turkish arthouse distributor Baska Sinema has acquired domestic theatrical rights to “A Woman Asleep,” an experimental English-language AI feature directed by pioneering artist and filmmaker Vikki Bardot. Bardot is considered one of the early practitioners of photographic AI art and video art. She delivered a TEDx talk on AI and art in 2023, and her artworks have been exhibited worldwide, including New York, Paris, London, Berlin, Rome and Miami. Her AI short “Dreamt by Another” screened in more than 40 festivals and was recently acquired by Mubi for Turkey . Related Stories 'Into the Breach' Review: Star-Studded British Theater Doc Needs More Time to Serve Its Sprawling Subject Matter 'Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Chris Pine and an All-Star Cast Play Space Aliens in David and Nathan Zellner’s Endearingly Goofy Sci-Fi Spoof “A Woman Asleep” is inspired by the 1974 cult French film “The Man Who Sleeps,” directed by Bernard Queysanne and Georges Perec. That movie, in turn, was based on Perec’s novel “A Man Asleep.” Popular on Variety In a rare occurrence, Bardot’s 80-minute AI drama that, according to the synopsis, examines contemporary alienation and numbness in today’s world of hyper-connectivity, is set for a spring 2027 release across 20 cities in Turkey via Baska Sinema. “A Woman Asleep” is produced by pioneering Turkish AI production studio Spongeworthy that is also behind buzzy AI-generated doc “Post Truth,” directed by Alkan Avcıoğlu which made a splash on the festival circuit and also, similarly, got a theatrical release via Baska Sinema in Turkey. The narration for “A Woman Asleep” is generated using an AI voice clone trained on the director’s own voice. “This choice extends the film’s conceptual framework and dreamlike qualities, allowing the narration to exist in a space between the human and the synthetic, consistent with the world the film portrays,” the promotional materials say, citing the storytelling approaches of Alain Resnais, Michelangelo Antonioni, Chris Marker and Apichatpong Weerasethakul as references. Edited from a pool of 50,000 individual shots, the experimental film took two years to complete. “I have been focused on AI filmmaking for 5 years, before it was even a popular subject in cinema,” said Bardot in a statement. “The most interesting use of AI isn’t recreating Hollywood forms. It’s giving independent filmmakers the freedom to make personal, formally ambitious films that might otherwise never get financed,” the director added. title: International Disruptors: Reta Guetg On Building Zurich Film Festival’s “Trendy” Identity & Why New Owners Want To Keep It Small, Nimble & Close To Hollywood
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Percy Hynes White & Jeff Wahlberg Lead Lovers-On-The-Run Thriller ‘Crime Novella’, Roland Emmerich Exec-Producing & First Look Revealed ‘The Lion King’ Director Rob Minkoff To Develop & Exec Produce Family Pic ‘Storm Dogs’ From Tilly Norwood Creator Particle 6 José Luis Rebordinos Reflects On His Final Year At San Sebastián: “What Surprises Me The Most Is How Much The Festival Has Grown” View All September 25, 2026 6:12am Reta Guetg Zurich Film Festival Welcome to Deadline’s International Disruptors , a feature where we shine a spotlight on key executives and companies outside of the U.S. shaking up the offshore marketplace. This week we’re talking to Zurich Film Festival Director & Co-Owner Reta Guetg about this year’s edition, her evolution at the festival and why she and fellow co-owners want to make it Europe’s trendiest festival. For someone who works in an industry that is constantly in flux, Zurich Film Festival Co-Owner and Festival Director Reta Guetg is resolute in her ambition for the young film event. Last year, she and ZFF CEO and Co-Owner Christian Jungen led a management buyout of the festival from newspaper publisher NZZ Group and this year the Swiss event is doubling down on a deliberately boutique identity, strengthening its relationship with Hollywood and positioning itself as a launchpad for awards contenders – all while using its industry flagship event, the Zurich Summit , to put emerging issues like AI at the center of the conversation. Related Stories News 'The Lion King' Director Rob Minkoff To Develop & Exec Produce Family Pic 'Storm Dogs' From Tilly Norwood Creator Particle 6 Festivals Zurich Summit 2026: FilmNation, AMPAS, Sony Classics, Mubi, Mattel, Komplizen, Mediawan, CAA, UTA, TikTok & YouTube Among Speakers At Swiss Conference “We’re not going to be an A-festival, that’s not our strategy,” Guetg tells Deadline. “We want to have the best films we can and push them to an audience, but also to the industry. We want to put them on the radar and be a relevant launchpad for awards contenders. We can be the perfect second home for a film to get visibility through a cool place like Zurich.” Watch on Deadline The 22 nd edition of ZFF kicked off on Thursday night with the European premiere of Mount Everest adventure Tenzing , starring Tom Hiddleston and Willem Dafoe and highlights in this year’s lineup include the European premiere of Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky as well as screenings of Naomi Watts starrer The Housewife and Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut . Further films set to screen at the 11-day event include Danny Boyle’s Ink , Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid , Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan starrer Josephine and Alexander Skarsgård and Olivia Colman rom-com Wicker . Talent in attendance this year include Hiddleston, Watts, McDonagh, Julianne Moore, Richard Linklater and John Turturro, all of whom are set to be feted by the fest. This weekend sees the return of its annual Zurich Summit, its flagship boutique industry conference that Guetg has been carefully building since she first joined ZFF in 2016. Running September 25-27, the summit is now renowned for attracting top Hollywood and international execs who descend upon the swanky Dolder Grand Hotel for the weekend to discuss current industry trends, issues and financing models. ZFF has dubbed it “the Davos of the film world” in reference to the annual World Economic Forum in the Swiss Alps. ZURICH, SWITZERLAND – OCTOBER 03: Christian Jungen, Amanda Seyfried and Reta Guetg attend the “The Testament Of Ann Lee” green carpet during the 21st Zurich Film Festival at Corso Green Carpet on October 03, 2025 in Zurich, Switzerland. (Photo by Joshua Sammer/Getty Images for ZFF) Last year, the event went viral when Tilly Norwood was introduced to the world during a Deadline-moderated panel with her creator Eline van der Velden. After reporting that a number of talent agents were circling the AI actress for representation , the story quickly sparked a global debate and firmly put Zurich at the forefront of the conversation. “The Tilly Norwood story really showed how Zurich can be relevant,” says Guetg. “We are a platform to launch a discussion for the industry that continued to be a discussion out of Zurich. That was really memorable and I think it was a sign that somehow, after all of these years, we are at the center of these important topics and ideas. It validated all that we have built over these years.” With wind in its sails, the Zurich Summit is ramping up its efforts this year. Attendees the 2026 event include FilmNation Entertainment CEO Glen Basner (who is receiving the annual Game Changer Award), Backrooms director Kane Parsons, AMPAS CEO Bill Kramer, CAA Media Finance Co-Heads Roeg Sutherland and Sarah Schweitzman, UTA Independent Film Group Partner and Head Rena Ronson, Mediawan Pictures CEO Elisabeth d’Arvieu and Mubi CEO Efe Cakarel. Van der Velden is also returning along with speakers from TikTok and YouTube. Guetg, who was first in charge of building the industry strand of the fest when she started at ZFF decade ago, points to its strong relationships with Hollywood – notably CAA – who have helped bring speakers to the confab each year. “We’ve had a lot of goodwill and help from Hollywood execs and agencies to help us grow this event – they are our soft power.” Its success, she says, is also down to its “boutique and bespoke” nature. “It’s one of the rare times, particularly in this busy fall season, where there’s less people,” says Guetg. “It’s very curated and it’s an environment where people really have time to sit down and talk to each other in different surroundings. I think this quality time makes a difference.” First steps Guetg’s route into the film business began in Bern in 2000 when she launched short film festival Shnit. “It grew quite quickly into a big thing in our hometown,” she says. “We built it from scratch, and our idea was to just show fun, short films in Bern. We had a very good community of really packed cinemas.” That festival quickly grew internationally, spanning to multiple cities including Cape Town, Bangkok and Cairo, among others, and Guetg said growing it was “intuitive.” “I learned so much by doing it and that’s really how I learned how to own my own business and be in charge of everything,” she says. “It was a super great school for me.” After a decade, Guetg felt it was time to move on and, after some production freelancing gigs, ZFF approached her to head up the festival’s burgeoning industry section. “Zurich had a similar history in terms that the founders just had an idea and went for it,” she says. “That felt so familiar to me. It was obviously a completely different size but this idea that nobody really waits for you and being a bit of an underdog – because Zurich did things differently to other festivals –, that felt very natural to me.” ZFF’s next phase It’s a pivotal time for ZFF now, which is notably entering a new chapter following a management buyout in July 2025. Guetg is one of the festival’s now five owners, alongside well-respected former artistic director Jungen (now ZFF CEO), entrepreneur and TV host Max Loong, longtime ZFF President Felix E. Müller and finance expert Marek Skreta. The move gave Guetg and her fellow owners greater control over the festival’s future after being owned by NZZ Group, publisher of Neue Zürcher Zeitung newspaper, for a decade. ZURICH, SWITZERLAND – SEPTEMBER 28: Reta Guetg, Tom Quinn, Christian Junger at the Zurich Summit Dinner during the 21st Zurich Film Festival at Restaurant Terrasse on September 28, 2025 in Zurich, Switzerland. (Photo by Andreas Rentz/Getty Images for ZFF) “It happened in July, almost three months before last year’s festival, so there was not much time to think about what it would really mean,” she says. “So, we had to regroup quite quickly after the festival with this new ownership and figure out where we wanted to go.” The response so far, she says, has been energizing. “It’s opened up a lot of motivation for all of us, including the team, festival friends or donors that support the festival – everyone liked the idea of having an independent group of people run it rather than a big corporation.” The priority is to retain what she describes as Zurich’s DNA: an ability to move quickly, experiment and take risks without becoming weighed down by its own scale. “We need to be so agile, and Zurich has always been quite adaptive, so it was important for us to keep the DNA of the festival.” She is clear that the ambition is not to scale up to the size of festivals like Cannes or Toronto. Instead, much like its summit, Guetg sees value in Zurich’s comparatively intimate scale. “That’s the idea – to keep it small. We don’t want to grow it into a huge event quantity-wise, that’s not the idea at all. We’re a very guest-friendly and talent-friendly city and we’re known for being good hosts.” ZFF has increasingly embraced its own position as a slightly unconventional European player. Guetg cites a 2022 Guardian article’s description of Zurich , which said: “If Venice and Cannes are the grandmothers of the European festival scene, ZFF is the trendy teenager.” The phrase, she says, has stuck. “This has become our vision – to be the trendiest film festival in Europe,” Guetg says. “And I think we’re quite near this.” She continues: “We’ve been lucky that people have been connecting us with people who are aligned with our vision of what we want Zurich to be. Looking ahead, I think it’s important that we try not to do everything, but we continue to try and get the right people. And also to continue to not be so risk averse, because that is more important than ever.” The 22 nd Zurich Film Festival runs September 24-October 4, 2026. ‘Avengers: Endgame: Encore’ & ‘Primetime’ Eye $3M Previews ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’, Meta Finale & Season 2 Judge Grants Suit Settlement Delay; Company Proceeds With $7.5B Debt Raise David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi; WBD’s CNN, MS Now Denied Access To Event Read More About: Comments

title: NASA Astronaut Victor Glover Signs With CAA (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 25, 2026 5:23am Artemis II NASA astronaut Victor Glover Courtesy of NASA NASA astronaut Victor Glover has signed with CAA for representation in all areas after he has retired as a space explorer. The Hollywood talent agency will look to expand opportunities for Glover in the unscripted TV and books and publishing spaces, as an event speaker and for brand endorsements and community impact. The signing follows Glover in spring 2026 piloting NASA’s Artemis II mission, and becoming the first Black astronaut to fly around the moon. That 10-day mission had Glover flying as far as 252,756 miles from Earth. Signing with CAA also follows Glover, a veteran naval aviator, test pilot and astronaut, stepping back from NASA to support future missions as part of the agency’s emeritus program. He has also joined the California Polytechnic State University, his alma mater, as an executive advisor. Glover received his Bachelor of Science in general engineering from Cal Poly, which along with Brown University awarded him honorary Doctor of Science degrees. Glover brings to the Hollywood talent agency a social media presence that includes around 532,000 Instagram followers and another 250,000-plus on the X platform. The retired U.S. Navy captain also piloted the first operational flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft, Resilience, to the International Space Station. He was first selected to become an astronaut in 2013 after serving as a test pilot for the F/A‐18 Hornet, Super Hornet and EA‐18G Growler aircraft. A native Californian, Glover also earned his Master of Science in flight test engineering and a Master of Military Operational Art and Science from Air University, and a Master of Science in systems engineering from the Naval Postgraduate School. title: BBC Boss Matt Brittin On Expected Service Closures: “No Program Or Channel Will Exist Forever”
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Boss Matt Brittin On Expected Service Closures: “No Program Or Channel Will Exist Forever” ‘Have I Got News For You’ Producer Torches BBC Investigation Into Victoria Beckham Joke As “Total Waste” Of Money BBC Rebukes ‘Have I Got News For You’ After Complaints About “Gratuitously Offensive” Victoria Beckham Joke View All September 25, 2026 5:12am BBC boss Matt Brittin on 'Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg' BBC News BBC director-general Matt Brittin has hinted that the broadcaster is preparing to close TV and radio networks as it looks to save money and better serve audiences online. In an interview that will air over the weekend, Brittin told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the BBC’s ambition to save £500 million ($662M) “may well mean” that services are shut. The former Google executive said the BBC “wouldn’t guarantee any program or any channel will exist forever. The tight financial situation means that we’re having to look at some of those decisions a bit sooner than we might like.” Related Stories News 'Have I Got News For You' Producer Torches BBC Investigation Into Victoria Beckham Joke As "Total Waste" Of Money News BBC Rebukes 'Have I Got News For You' After Complaints About "Gratuitously Offensive" Victoria Beckham Joke Brittin’s comments follow Deadline reporting on Wednesday that the BBC is expected to announce the closure of TV and radio networks as early as next week. There is speculation about the future of BBC Three, but nothing is confirmed at this stage. When’s the right time to migrate that service fully to being on demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer.” He added that the BBC had to go “in different ways to reach audiences and we’re locked into yesterday’s model of how people consume content and actually the audience is always already living in tomorrow’s world.” The BBC’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap. Sally Habbershaw is exiting Mediawan after less than a year to become President of Global Distribution at the BBC’s commercial arm. Her London-based role will see her overseeing BBCS’s worldwide content sales business, reporting into Zai Bennett, BBC Studios Global Content CEO and Chief Creative Officer. BBC Studios has been without a sales boss for most of the year, as the U.S.-based Janet Brown exited in January as part of a plan to move distribution closer to the mothership in the UK. Habbershaw takes up her “newly expanded” post on September 29. Related Stories News 'Doctor Who' Re-Gen Is Go! title: Tales Of Syria’s Disappeared; Lebanese Wartime Adoption & Palestinian Mental Health Set For Cinemed-Aflamuna Project Incubator
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Tales Of Syria’s Disappeared; Lebanese Wartime Adoption & Palestinian Mental Health Set For Cinemed-Aflamuna Project Incubator Netflix-Acquired Animation ‘In Waves’ To Open The American French Film Festival In L.A. CAPA Deputy Director Unveils Sean Connery Doc; Talks Mission To Expand French Company’s International Reach View All September 25, 2026 2:26am Cinemed- Aflamuna pitching session Cinemed France ’s Montpellier Mediterranean Film Festival, also known as Cinemed , and Beirut-based Arab cinema platform Aflamuna have unveiled the selection for their fifth project incubator event, which will take place within the framework of the festival in October. The initiative, bannered the Aflamuna x Cinemed Encounters and supporting Arab filmmakers from across the Middle East and Africa, will showcase seven projects. They include the documentary Disappeared following five Syrian women as they come to terms with the forced disappearance of their sons and husbands under the Bashar Al-Asaad regime, without ever giving up the search for their fate. Related Stories News CAPA Deputy Director Unveils Sean Connery Doc; Talks Mission To Expand French Company's International Reach Festivals The Guardian To Offer 'NAZA' For Free On Website From November After Theatrical Run & Is Exploring Ways To Show Doc In Israel & Palestinian Territories The work taps into a raw subject in Syria where at least 177,000 people remain missing having been forcibly disappeared by the regime from 2011 onwards. Watch on Deadline It is the latest film from Palestinian, Syria-raised director Anas Zawahri, who made waves this year with My Memory Is Full of Ghosts , revisiting the war-ravaged Syrian city of Homs in 2023, prior to the overthrowing of Al-Assad in December 2024. Further projects in the selection include Palestinian Wisam Al Jafari’s The Hearse to the Final House of Happiness , about a mental patient who is granted a brief leave from the institution where he is being cared for to attend a family wedding. It is Al Jafari’s debut feature after award-winning shorts Ambience (2019), By The Sea (2021), Cinema, Mon Amour (2026.) Hanna Attallah is producing under his Route 243 banner after credits including Thank You for Banking with Us by Laila Abbas, which played multiple festivals including the BFI London Film Festival. Cinemed and Aflamuna launched their joint project incubator in 2021, with the support of France’s National Cinema Center (CNC), to support filmmakers in 22 Arab territories in the Middle East and Africa, Under the initiative the participants attend Cinemed’s professional days, running from October 20 to 22 this year, where they French and international professionals and decision-makers for potential partnerships. “After five years, the Aflamuna x Cinemed Encounters, in the continuity of the Aflamuna connection program, are now a well-established part of the Cinemed Meetings, attracting a vast network of producers, French and European institutions interested in discovering new projects from the Arab world,” said Cinemed director Christophe LeParc. “We are proud to present the seven projects selected this year, and to help expanding their reach and visibility in European markets.” Cinemed runs from October 16 to 24. The 2026 Aflamuna x Cinemed Encounters Selection A Tale of a Feather and a Fish ( Egypt ) Dir. Ahmed El Hawarey Prods . Hala Lotfy (Hassala Films), Jeanne Deny (MAD Solutions) Amidst the shadow of a devastating genetic disease, three broken family members struggle to find salvation; they are guided toward healing by the very loved ones they must care for. Accept My Plea For Burial ( Somalia /Djibouti) Dir. Mohammed Sheikh Prod. Kadir Harbi, producer (Aleel Films) In a remote Somali pastoral village, two twelve-year-old boys, Waasuge and Warmooge, spend their days herding goats and playing. Their rivalry turns tragic when Warmooge dies after falling into a dry riverbed during a game. With no clear witness and conflicting testimonies, suspicion grows. As grief turns to accusation, Warmooge’s mother refuses burial without justice, and the village fractures under the weight of uncertainty and pressure to resolve the truth. Disappeared (doc) France-Syria- Lebanon -Iraq Dir. Anas Zawahri Prod. Ahmad Al Haj (Wind Cinéma) Five Syrian women confront the forced disappearance of their sons and husbands. Through their daily lives and an ongoing search for truth, they resist political erasure, preserve memory, and reclaim meaning within their cities in the Syrian marginalized countryside. I Have Other Friends (doc) Egypt Dir. Yomna Khattab Prod. Muhammad Taymour (Chaos Films) Yomna, the director, on the verge of turning forty, takes us on a personal, intimate journey to portray her female best friends. By navigating the difficult postponed conversations with them, Yomna wonders: ‘Who are my friends when I hit forties?’ The Hearse to the Final House of Happiness Palestine Dir. Wisam Al Jafari Prod . Hanna Attallah (Route 243) When a Palestinian mental patient in his fifties is granted a brief leave to attend a family wedding, the event descends into chaotic absurdity as his political obsession, a restless family, and street protests clash. The Space I Carry (doc) Lebanon-France Dir. Élise Pouchelet, Codirector and producer . Josef Khallouf (The FilmMonk) Born in Lebanon in 1975, at the beginning of the Civil War, Elise was abandoned, then adopted, and carried away to France. Fifty years later, she traces the two lineages that run through her, feeling her way through the fragments and silences that have quietly shaped her. It is in the solitude of the mountains, in the company of wild things, that she finally learns to inhabit the space she carries. Twelve Fig Leaves (doc) Lebanon Dir. Joëlle Abou Chabké Prod. Lara Abou Saïfan (Placeless films) When filmmaker-turned-farmer Joëlle discovers the Bawāhīr, an ancestral Lebanese method of weather prediction, she embarks on a year-long journey to test its accuracy while building a permaculture project with her husband in his native Bekaa village.
