In Episode 6 of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe, the quartet of accidental heroes Stuart Bloom ( Kevin Sussman ), Denise ( Lauren Lapkus ), Bert (Brian Posehn) and Barry Kripke (John Ross Bowie) find themselves in a universe where people have descended from cows; they eat plants and chew their cud. Kripke and Bert want to leave, Stuart and Denise opt to stay, leading to the former duo being stuck falling in an endless void in-between universes. After meeting a new version of Raj (Kunal Nayyar) — who does not mention the broken device his post-apocalyptic self almost fixed in the first episode — and getting scolded by Stuart from another dimension, Stuart and Denise somehow order a second copy of the machine and soon find themselves falling through the void alongside Kripke and Bert. Related Stories News 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' Creators On Magic Of Returning To 'Big Bang' Stage, Going Multi-Cam In Meta Season 1 Finale & Season 2 Plans News Olivia Wilde's A24 Relationship Dramedy 'The Invite' Sets HBO Max Premiere Date Turns out the horror on their faces was not just acting but the screams were hard to muster, Sussman and Lapkus told Deadline. “There were so many things that were crazy, I think being in the Matrix was insane, we were all with our bald caps in goo pods, and then we were on high wires, like flying, being dropped 30 feet in the air to shoot the falling-through-the-void scene, that was very scary,” Lapkus said about their experience filming Season 1 of the Big Bang Theory spinoff. “The high wire one in particular, the scene was we’re being dropped, falling through the air, and we’re supposed to be screaming,” Sussman said. “And what Lauren and I discovered both simultaneously the first time we were dropped, it was so much faster and scarier than we thought that neither of us were able to scream.” Added Lapkus, “When you’re actually scared, you can’t scream. It’s kind of like those nightmares that I’ve had over and over again, where I’m trying to scream and I can’t. When you’re falling and you’re actually scared, you just swallow it, we’re choking. Yeah, it was terrifying.” (You can watch the video below.) title: ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Magic Of Returning To ‘Big Bang’ Stage, Going Multi-Cam In Meta Season 1 Finale & Season 2 Plans
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Magic Of Returning To ‘Big Bang’ Stage, Going Multi-Cam In Meta Season 1 Finale & Season 2 Plans ‘The Beast In Me’ Renewed For Season 2 With Claire Danes Reprising Role; Howard Gordon Back With Netflix Overall Deal David Oyelowo & Viola Prettejohn To Star In ‘The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo’ TV Series For Sky View All September 24, 2026 6:25pm Story Arc (L-R): Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman, John Ross Bowie & Brian Posehn in 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' S1 finale HBO Max SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about the Season 1 finale “Spoiler: Filmed In Front Of a Live Studio Audience” of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe . The Big Bang Theory single-camera spinoff Stuart Fails To Save the Universe went full-circle in the Season 1 finale by turning multi-camera and returning to the stage where the original series was filmed. After getting trapped in a comic book in the penultimate episode, the multiverse-hopping quartet of Stuart (Kevin Sussman), Bert (Brian Posehn), Denise (Lauren Lapkus) and Kripke (John Ross Bowie) found themself in a multi-camera sitcom in the finale, complete with a laugh track. Related Stories News How 'All American' Survived Long Enough To End Its 8-Season Run As The Lone YA Series Left At The CW: An Oral History Agencies Ari Emanuel On His New Memoir, Nikki Finke, Talking To Trump, AI's Upside & The Hollywood Exec He Hates The Most And, in the trippiest moment in a season chockfull of meta references, in the finale, Stuart, Denise, Bert and Kripke witnessed a curtain call for a taping of the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe sitcom where they see identical versions of themselves played by the real-life stars of the HBO Max series: Sussman, Posehn, Lapkus and Bowie. Watch on Deadline Still shocked, the four walked out of the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe soundstage, which is revealed to be Stage 25 on the Warner Bros. lot that housed Big Bang. (The stage is currently home to CBS spinoff Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage, which co-creator Lorre and Prady executive produce.) “So now what?,” Denise asked in the final seconds of the episode. “I don’t know but I’ve got to believe that the answer is out there somewhere,” Stuart said in a X-Files -esque “The truth is out there” manner, prompting Bert to follow up with “In Burbank?” and Kevin to reply, “or Studio City?,” a reference to the city Warner Bros. is based in and the neighboring area. The finale’s back-and-forth shift between single- and multi-camera involved Stuart Fails To Save the Universe building a multi-camera version of Stuart’s comic book like the one used in Big Bang on the Universal lot where the Warner Bros. TV-produced Big Bang spinoff films its interiors and some exteriors. (The final exterior scene was filmed outside of the real Stage 25 on the Warners lot.) The episode paid homage to the mothership series in other ways too, including incorporating Big Bang ‘s signature animated atom transition, complete with the whooshing sound, using its audience warm-up Mark Sweet, who had worked with Lorre since his 1997 ABC comedy Dharma & Greg, and having the characters sit around a coffee table eating takeouts. In an interview with Deadline, the Stuart Fails creators/executive producers Zak Penn , who comes from genre background, and sitcom veterans Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady , break down how they pulled off the single-camera/multi-camera transitions, how it was filming outside Stage 25, the various Big Bang easter eggs and that ending (where exactly is the answer?). They also address the several digs at CBS, broadcast television and multi-camera sitcoms, the black consciousness adversary introduced in the finale and its implied alliance with Kyle (Ryan Cartwright). The trio gives some clues about the recently picked up Season 2, which already is being written, including when it would premiere. How ‘Stuart’ Brought ‘Big Bang’ (& Its Laugh) Back DEADLINE: Where did the idea to have our heroes be in a multi-camera sitcom come about? Did you want to pay homage to Big Bang? PENN : Yeah, that was definitely part of it. These guys [Lorre and Prady] have a lot to say about it, so it was pretty fertile ground. I don’t think we said at the beginning of the season, we must comment on the sitcom, that wasn’t a goal. LORRE : If our characters on their adventure, on their journey, could be trapped into a comic book, they could certainly be trapped into a sitcom. I mean, we’ve gone past any boundaries of rationale, and this is a spectacularly cool thing to do, let’s do it. Can we explain it? We’re gonna try, we’re certainly going to try. DEADLINE: You used both single-camera and multi-camera versions of the comic book set in the episode. For the multi-cam one that you had to build, did you use any pieces of the original Big Bang set? PRADY : We didn’t use the original sets, but you’re right, we had to build. The only way to do this, because a multi-cam set looks different than a single-cam set, is we had to build the set two times. We had our single-cam comic book store that we’ve been using all season with four walls and a ceiling, and on the next stage over at Universal, they built the multi-cam version of that set and the multi-cam version of the stockroom. But they also had to build the interior of a multi-cam soundstage, they had to build audience risers, the sound booth and the lighting booth that sits behind the audience, the camera alley, all of those features of multi-cam stage, they had to build. Our amazing production team actually went over to Georgie and Mandy, which was in production at the time, so that they could copy it and and get it right. And it was also a change for the director of photography. The camera moves in multi-cam are completely different, the cameras go onto dollies, you have dolly moves that don’t exist in single-cam, and all of that had to be duplicated. So it was a pretty, pretty complicated task. DEADLINE: How many scenes did you have to film twice in both formats? There were scenes that switched between single- and multi-cam. PENN: Probably one third, two thirds, maybe more single-cam. Every time you see that, we had to do it twice, we had to shoot it on both stages, but there wasn’t a live studio audience there for that part of it. The live studio audience was only there when we needed to see the live studio audience. LORRE : For the curtain call. PENN : Because it would have been so boring to watch these little snippets of scenes, it just wouldn’t have made sense to anyone. DEADLINE: Bert makes a comment on the show that the laugh is fake. You just said that the live studio audience was not used for the actual taping of the scenes beyond the curtain call, so the spoiler in the episode’s title is not accurate. PRADY : It’s pretty perverse. One of the things that we battled forever on Big Bang Theory was people saying that this was a laugh track when it was a live studio audience. So here, in fact, the laughter that you’re hearing during the scene, the laugh that Kripke is hearing, those are old laughs from a The Big Bang Theory audience eight or nine years ago. Yes, all of those ironies. (L-R): Ryan Cartwright, Brian Posehn, Kevin Sussman, Lauren Lapkus & John Ross Bowie in ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ S1 finale HBO Max Dinging CBS As “Old TV Thing”, Sitcoms As “Void” DEADLINE: Speaking of ironies, the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe sitcom within the series is promoted as “Coming to CBS this fall.” Is this just a line of dialogue, or is there some truth here? Can you license this show to CBS, home of Big Bang and all other spinoffs, for a linear run? LORRE : That’s a question you’d have to ask HBO. I wouldn’t think so. It was just an opportunity to make a cheap joke about the end of network television. DEADLINE: Yes, the punchline to that was Kyle asking “What is CBS?”, and Kripke explaining it as an “old TV thing,” a dig at broadcast and CBS. Did you write that, Chuck? They’re still employing you. LORRE : I want to bite the hand that feeds me, Elvis Costello. DEADLINE: There was another shot, about a meaningless void and sitcoms being the same thing. Is this how you all feel about multi-cam comedies these days? LORRE : Not at all. No, it was a joke, Nellie. It was an opportunity to try and make the audience laugh. PRADY : It’s certainly what Kripke thinks. LORRE : It might be what Kripke thinks of situation comedies, but the history of this genre is just rich with genius, going back to Lucy and Norman Lear and Cheers and Friends and Frasier. It’s ridiculous to try and put down a genre that has done such great work over decades. PRADY : We’re in awe of the genre. LORRE : It’s much harder to do this than it is to shoot a little movie. It’s much harder to make 200 people laugh, even if they’re related to you. DEADLINE: Chuck, any plans to do another multi-cam sitcom? I saw CBS Entertainment President Amy Reisenbach recently, and she said that the door is wide open for you . LORRE : That’s very sweet of her. I love that woman. I’ve been doing this an awful long time, and Amy is just terrific. She’s been a really big supporter of Georgie and Mandy out of the gate, she’s been nothing but helpful and supportive of us trying to put on a show. DEADLINE: But no current plans for you to do a new sitcom? LORRE : No. My current plans are to take a nap right after we’re done talking. (L-R): Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie in ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ S1 finale Behind The Curtain Call DEADLINE: The level of meta play in the finale — I don’t know if mushrooms or something else was involved in coming up with the sitcom idea, but the idea to have… LORRE : It’s not drugs, it is called imagination. It’s something that will go away shortly with the advent of AI sitcoms. But, for the time being, it’s making sh*t up is what’s happening. DEADLINE: But the idea to have the characters looking at actors carrying their real names playing the same characters; talk about how this whole thing made sense. PENN : This is a place that we hadn’t gone, and going there seemed kind of scary, like, how are we going to make this work? And then, how are we going to write our way out of it? I think that was the approach the whole season is what something we could do that would be funny, but also, let’s not just do oh, and now they go to a universe where everybody’s a bird or whatever, like trying to come up with something to top what we had done, and this seemed like the place to go. DEADLINE: Did Brian pay extra because everyone got a straightforward intro when Mark Sweet brought out the cast, he’s the only one who got “hilariously funny”? PRADY : So the cast is allowed to bribe us, and we have a whole set. PENN : Yeah, Brian paid us, you’re right. Brian gave us $1,500, and the rest of the cast gave us like 100 bucks, or someone gave us wine. We couldn’t split it. That was Mark Sweet, right? Whatever he chose to say. PRADY : We were writing the kinds of things Mark Sweet said, which, when we sat down to write it, Chuck and I had heard it so many times, we channeled Mark Sweet, who’s playing himself as the audience warm-up guy, without even thinking about it. LORRE : It was really easy. We’ve been listening to Mark since 1996, since Dharma & Greg . Thirty years, he’s been doing the same act. PRADY : He’s got turns of phrase like, “you know him, you love him.” There’s a whole bunch of stuff that we just know. It’s years of listening to Mark and literally writing what we’ve heard him say. (L-R): John Ross Bowie, Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman & Brian Posehn in ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ S1 finale HBO Max The Magic Of Stage 25 DEADLINE: You filmed the final scene outside of WB’s Stage 25, where Big Bang was shot. How was that? LORRE : That was a fun night. DEADLINE: Was it really rainy, or did you make everything wet? PENN : No, that’s a classic wet-town. LORRE : I loved how we ended it. It’s a really delicate thing to bring a season to an end, or a series to an end, which we’ve certainly been through. It’s a real lot of hoping and wishing and praying that you get it right. I thought we brought the 10 episodes to a wonderful — hopefully, a reason to anticipate Season 2 as well as pleasurable to watch. PENN : There was a bit of magic that night, watching the actors walk out through that door and onto the lot. It definitely felt there was something in the air. LORRE : Yeah, something special happened that night. PRADY : What was really strange that night, because we were shot at Stage 25, which was obviously the Big Bang stage, and walking in and using that stage, like using that as a place to stand and as a place to use the restroom and stuff. I found it very surreal, personally, to walk onto stage 25 with all that muscle memory of the years of Big Bang. 12 years there. The Answer, The Adversary & ‘Young Leonard’ DEADLINE: Speaking of the ending, the final line “I’ve got to believe that the answer is out there.” Was that an X-Files reference? LORRE : It does echo a little bit of The X-Files , doesn’t it? “The answer is out there, in Burbank, or maybe Studio City.” Yeah, it is something of a variation on that, I suppose, I hadn’t really thought about it. PRADY : Not on purpose. LORRE : Just a chance to say Burbank, because whenever you get a chance to say Burbank, you should. DEADLINE: So where is the answer? Is it in Burbank, in Studio City or somewhere else? LORRE : The answer is in Episode 1 of Season 2. DEADLINE: The adversary, that whole swirly consciousness thing we saw at the end, do we know what it is? Don’t tell me the answer is going to be in 201. PENN : The answer will be in 201. DEADLINE: Is Ryan’s character working for the adversary? Because the thing said to him “I gave you one job.” Is Kyle a bad guy? PENN : That version of those two characters work for the adversary. PRADY : But not all versions. PENN : But not the other ones you’ve seen that season. And then there’s another group led by, as far as you know, led by Stuart Prime. That’s the Stuart who shows up periodically to give them clues or hints to try to help them on their way. DEADLINE: Would that be a major point in Season 2 , who’s behind this? PENN : Unquestionably, it’s going to be dealt with. We didn’t want to spend the whole season doing a bunch of mythology shows where we break down every single thing about what’s going on. We just wanted to set some stuff up. LORRE : The truth is out there. DEADLINE: The final shot includes banners for Two and a Half Women and Young Leonard . Chuck, were there spoofs of any of your other sitcoms’ titles that you considered and discarded? LORRE : I don’t think so. I think, just the idea that we’re not quite in the universe where we started this series is the implication of those posters. PRADY : It’s not quite our world. LORRE : It’s close. PRADY : But also in this world, Stuart is a multi-cam as opposed to in our world where it’s a single-cam. So we wanted to show that we were two or three degrees off of our universe. DEADLINE: Two and a Half Women and Young Leonard are not bad ideas. Have Warner Bros. TV executive reached out about possibly doing them as shows? LORRE : No, they haven’t come to us with anything like that, nor should they. (L-R): Kevin Sussman & Lauren Lapkus in ‘Stuart Fails To Save the Universe’ S1 finale HBO Max Season 2: Everything We Know DEADLINE: You are in the writers’ room, right? Have you already mapped out Season 2? LORRE : We started working last week on fleshing out Season 2, which hopefully, I think production begins in January or February. Like Season 1, we’re hoping to write all the episodes before we start, giving all the departments a lot of lead time to do the remarkable stuff they did in Season 1, which was truly benefited also by us being allowed to stay in Los Angeles and do this here with the best crews in the world. PRADY : Yeah, it’s worth saying in every episode that we had the most amazing production team: sets, costumes, props, art direction, photography, lighting, sound. Every person on that stage was a gift, and everyone’s coming back. LORRE : Yeah, everybody’s coming back. One of the little miracles that happened was we got a tax break from the state of California, which allowed us to stay here, stay in Los Angeles, which allowed us to have the best crews. DEADLINE: Can you do the show on yearly cadence? There are a lot of special effects but can Season 2 premiere next summer or next fall? When will it be ready? LORRE : We’re hoping certainly by next fall. We’re shooting to also participate in Comic-Con again next year. We did it this year, and it was great, it was a great way to launch the first season. When the show actually will debut on HBO, we don’t know. But hopefully, we’ll at least have an episode or two finished to do Comic Con. PENN : It’s not going to be like two years between seasons. It’s going to come out next year. LORRE : Next year, yeah. DEADLINE: Will Season 2 be similar in structure, the gang going to a new universe each episode or will you revisit some of the more popular worlds from the first season? LORRE : We’ll try and put together 10 great episodes, and that’s the goal, to not run dry. PRADY : You don’t have to follow a strict rule. LORRE : You can return to a universe, there’s no rule against that. We’re not bound to say we couldn’t go back to some place they’ve already been if there was a great reason to do so. PRADY : Right. We don’t sit here and say okay, well we have to do fan service, so more centaurs. But if more centaurs is really funny and has a story that can be told, then there’ll be more centaurs. But we make fun of our own mythology as we’re going, so I think there’s no real rules about what we’re going to do. We just try to do something that’s interesting. DEADLINE: Will you also keep the idea of original Big Bang stars coming back? And I assume that the characters of Leonard, Howard, and Sheldon will stay off limits because if one of them shows up, he will fix the machine, and its show will be over. LORRE : We’re hopeful that we can have some guest starring opportunities again in Season 2, but we haven’t figured that out quite yet. It was a lot of fun working with Mayim [Bialik] and Melissa [Rauch], Kunal [Nayyar], Kaley [Cuoco]. Having them do something that they never did on The Big Bang Theory , giving them an opportunity to stretch a little bit, that’s been built into this from the beginning, and I hope we can keep it going. DEADLINE: Is there any chance of seeing different versions of Jim Parsons’ Sheldon, Johnny Galecki’s Leonard or Simon Helberg’s Howard ? PRADY : Tune in next season. LORRE : There’s always a chance. We’re not going to limit ourselves as to cameos. If it’s possible and it can be done, great. That was a lot of fun for us, and I think it was a lot of fun for the folks who came and played with us for a couple of days. DEADLINE: What’s the verdict on the custom opening credits? Have fans liked it, skipped it, didn’t care? Will you keep that in Season 2? LORRE : I haven’t talked to fans recently but we enjoyed it, we thought it was funny. PRADY : Our families liked it. LORRE : We thought it was adding value to the show to have different credits, different opening titles every week and break some rules with what we’re used to seeing on all television. PRADY : Maybe we’ll mix it up and, if we can come up with something even crazier, maybe we’ll do that. But don’t quote me on that. DEADLINE: Length-wise, will you keep the episodes brisk and short again next season? [Half of the Season 1 episodes, including the finale, were 15-18 min each ] LORRE : As long as they need to be. And I’m keeping my fingers crossed that some of these shorter episodes we can get on Quibi. PRADY : That has been the goal from the beginning. LORRE : Because kids want to watch these shows on their phones while they’re at the supermarket. That was pitched to me. DEADLINE: Quibi was ahead of its time, let’s just say that. LORRE (sarcastically): Sure. Lessons Learned DEADLINE: What did you learn from the first season? Anything that you want to do differently in Season 2? PENN : I learned a lot about sitcoms personally. LORRE : Special effects take a long time. PRADY : Be patient with special effects. LORRE : Be very patient. I had panic attacks all through Season 1 that some of the special effects that we were asking for were not going to work. They all did but it took time. It’s an arduous process to build stuff that doesn’t exist. PENN : That was the part I was comfortable with. LORRE : He is very comfortable with it; Zak said, It’ll be fine, it’ll be fine. Just let them, It’s not finished yet. It was the thing you hear over and over and over again but it was really gratifying when that stuff works. PENN : There wasn’t a lot that didn’t work, honestly. People might like some episodes more than others. LORRE : That’s inevitable. PENN : But normally, in doing a sci-fi show, you would find like, oh, we couldn’t pull this off, but that never happened to us. I mean, everything got pulled off. The crew, we say it over and over again, but they nailed it. There was never an episode where we walked in and said, Okay, the departments couldn’t really make this work. Let’s write around it. Never happened. LORRE : It took quite a bit for us to figure out how to do the falling through the void sequence, but we got there. There was some trial and error because we didn’t know. It’s one thing to write on a laptop, the character Bert and and Kripke are falling through an endless void, it’s easy to write down. It’s much more difficult to make it a reality, and I think ultimately we got there. DEADLINE: Uh-huh. Ask your actors, they told me they were traumatized filming that scene . PRADY : Well, that was another benefit. LORRE : Traumatized is part of show business. PRADY : I do know that the actors, in all their interviews, kept saying there was a lot more running, they found a lot more running than they thought. title: Disney Legal Chief Warns Of “Hard Choices” & “Much Smaller Organization” Coming As Company Layoffs Loom
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition” Disney Legal Chief Warns Of “Hard Choices” & “Much Smaller Organization” Coming As Company Layoffs Loom No ParaBros Decision Today As Judge Delays Settlement Sign-Off; CA AG’s Office Insists Deal “Not The Result Of Collusion” View All September 24, 2026 7:40pm Disney Chief Legal Officer Horacio Gutierrez, WDC logo Disney EXCLUSIVE: An end-of-week memo from Disney ‘s Chief Legal and Global Affairs Officer has given an blunt warning that layoffs are coming amidst a “transformation process” that includes “automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies.” Without actually saying that AI is taking over or that job losses are on the horizon, the memo by Horacio Gutierrez strongly implies that. Sent out at noon on Sept. 18 to the LGA department, which counts less than 1,000 members globally, the missive has taken on a life of its own. It is being circulated among the Disney rank and file, with many fearing that the unsentimental message to LGA staffers applies to them too as they are bracing for rounds of layoffs, expected to begin as early as next week. Unspecified cuts within the LGA department are not connected to the next round of cuts, I hear. Related Stories News Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Blames Bob Iger For Ouster In New Memoir News Disney Hikes Price Of Disney+ And Hulu Streaming Plans The memo has also been shared throughout the entertainment law community in L.A., NYC and DC. Watch on Deadline Noting that the Mouse House’s “legal, government relations, operations, and others, are going through their own reinvention as technology reshapes how work gets done, and the operating models that underpin those professions,” the multi-tasked Gutierrez says he’s “taking a dispassionate look at every aspect of how we do our work, so we can do it in a more efficient and cost-effective manner.” Gutierrez joined Disney from Spotify in late 2021 under Bob Chapek ‘s short-lived reign as CEO. Replacing Disney veteran Alan Braverman in the top in-house legal job, Gutierrez was one of few key Chapek lieutenants to keep his job when Bob Iger returned as CEO in late 2022. “Obviously, this will require hard choices about where and how we deploy our resources and investments, including our staffing investments and how we work will look different in the months and years ahead,” Gutierrez writes in the memo, adding, “LGA will be a much smaller organization than it is today, and some of you will personally be affected by decisions we make in this process. As a result, we’ll have to consider a whole range of new models for different workloads, including automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies, moving to self-service models where appropriate, engaging alternative legal providers and others, and new expanded share services, even outsourcing.” Proving once again that timing is everything in this town, Gutierrez’s memo came on the same day that Disney unveiled Karandeep Anand as the company’s very first Chief Technology Officer. The ex- Character.AI , CEO will report directly to Disney boss Josh D’Amaro. With the most recent rounds of job cuts hitting Disney in April and then July, execs made no secret on the Aug. 5 earnings call that more are to come. To that, Gutierrez’s email also came as the deadline was looming for qualifying longtime Disney executives to take the company’s voluntary early retirement offer, first unveiled in August by EVP and Chief People Officer Sonia Coleman. The process was always expected to be followed by involuntary layoffs. Cutting to the chase in his September 18 memo and invoking the name of D’Amaro, Gutierrez goes on to tell his staff that “when teams work smarter, Disney can serve more fans at lower costs, freeing up capital to reinvest in the content, guest experiences, and technology infrastructure that keep the company out in front. “Josh’s vision is of a Disney that succeeds in a changing market by breaking internal walls and embracing technology to amplify what makes it great, not by clinging to the way things always have been done.” Disney would not comment on Gutierrez’s memo or on a timeline and scope of the upcoming job cuts when contacted Thursday by Deadline.
